\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 1\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">HEMORRHAGIC STROKE MANAGEMENT\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">These notes combine your two hemorrhagic stroke drafts, but I have corrected the parts that\u003cbr>should not be overused clinically. The key correction is this: CHA₂DS₂-VASc is not used for\u003cbr>acute hemorrhagic stroke management, and NIHSS is not the main hemorrhagic stroke decision-\u003cbr>making score. In acute intracerebral hemorrhage, the most important clinical decision tools are\u003cbr>GCS, CT findings, hematoma volume/location, intraventricular extension, hydrocephalus, mass\u003cbr>effect, anticoagulant use, and ICH score.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hemorrhagic stroke is an acute neurological deficit caused by bleeding within the cranial cavity.\u003cbr>It is mainly divided into intracerebral hemorrhage, where bleeding occurs into the brain\u003cbr>parenchyma, and subarachnoid hemorrhage, where bleeding occurs into the subarachnoid space,\u003cbr>commonly due to aneurysmal rupture.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This master note focuses on spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage, because this is the common\u003cbr>hypertensive hemorrhagic stroke usually managed in internal medicine, emergencies, ICU, and\u003cbr>neurosurgical settings. The 2022 AHA/ASA guideline defines spontaneous intracerebral\u003cbr>hemorrhage as non-traumatic bleeding into the brain parenchyma and emphasizes rapid\u003cbr>diagnosis, BP control, reversal of coagulopathy, neurosurgical assessment, ICP management, and\u003cbr>stroke-unit/ICU care.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 2\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hemorrhagic stroke kills through two mechanisms. First, the hematoma directly destroys brain\u003cbr>tissue. Second, the expanding hematoma causes raised intracranial pressure, perihematomal\u003cbr>edema, hydrocephalus, midline shift, herniation, and brainstem compression. The\u003cbr>AHA/ASA clinical update describes early injury from hematoma expansion and later secondary\u003cbr>injury from edema, inflammation, and blood product toxicity.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Common Causes of Hemorrhagic Stroke\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The commonest cause in many African/Tanzania ward settings is poorly controlled chronic\u003cbr>hypertension, especially with poor adherence to antihypertensive medication. Hypertensive\u003cbr>hemorrhage classically occurs in deep brain structures supplied by small penetrating arteries.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Important causes include:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Cause\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Typical clue\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Chronic hypertension\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Deep hemorrhage: basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Cerebral amyloid angiopathy\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Elderly patient, lobar hemorrhage\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Warfarin/DOAC/heparin\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Anticoagulant history, high INR if warfarin\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Antiplatelet therapy\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Aspirin/clopidogrel may worsen bleeding\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>AVM/aneurysm/cavernoma\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Young patient, lobar/unusual site, SAH component\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Brain tumor bleed\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Lobar hemorrhage with edema/mass lesion\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Liver disease, DIC, hematologic disease\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Cocaine/amphetamine\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Severe acute hypertension, young patient\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Hemorrhagic transformation\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Recent ischemic stroke/thrombolysis/large infarct\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In KCMC/Tanzania practical assessment, first ask about hypertension, adherence,\u003cbr>anticoagulants, antiplatelets, alcohol, CKD, trauma, previous stroke, and age. In a young\u003cbr>patient, lobar bleed, or unusual location, think harder about AVM, aneurysm, venous thrombosis,\u003cbr>tumor, or vasculitis.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. Clinical Presentation\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hemorrhagic stroke may present with sudden focal neurological deficit, severe headache,\u003cbr>vomiting, seizures, reduced consciousness, severe hypertension, or signs of raised intracranial\u003cbr>pressure. Compared with ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke more commonly presents with\u003cbr>headache, vomiting, early reduced GCS, seizures, and very high BP, although clinical features\u003cbr>alone cannot reliably differentiate the two.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Site-based clinical clues\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Hemorrhage site\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Clinical pattern\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 3\u003c/div>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Basal ganglia/internal\u003cbr>capsule\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Contralateral hemiparesis, facial weakness, sensory loss, gaze\u003cbr>deviation\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Thalamus\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Sensory loss, reduced consciousness, vertical gaze palsy\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Cerebellum\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Vomiting, vertigo, ataxia, headache, rapid deterioration if\u003cbr>hydrocephalus\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Pons\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Coma, pinpoint pupils, quadriparesis, abnormal respiration\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Lobar cortex\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Seizures, aphasia, neglect, visual field defect depending on lobe\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Intraventricular extension\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Reduced GCS, hydrocephalus, raised ICP\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Cerebellar and pontine hemorrhages are especially dangerous because small volumes can rapidly  compress the brainstem.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">5. Immediate Diagnostic Evaluation\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 1: Start with ABCDE\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Do not begin by writing a long clerking note. Start by deciding whether the patient is dying.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">A — Airway\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Assess whether the patient can protect the airway. Call ICU/anesthesia early if there is:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>GCS ≤8,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>recurrent vomiting,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>aspiration risk,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>bulbar dysfunction,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>uncontrolled seizures,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>brainstem signs,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>worsening consciousness.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If airway is unsafe, intubation may be required before CT.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">B — Breathing\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Check respiratory rate, SpO₂, breathing pattern, aspiration, and chest findings. Give oxygen if\u003cbr>hypoxic. Avoid hypoxia and hypercapnia because both increase secondary brain injury and may\u003cbr>worsen ICP.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Usual target SpO₂ is &gt;94%, but if COPD/CO₂ retention risk is present, use 88–92%.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">C — Circulation\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Insert two IV lines. Monitor BP, pulse, ECG, capillary refill, temperature, and urine output.\u003cbr>Avoid hypotension because it worsens cerebral perfusion. Use isotonic fluids if needed. Avoid\u003cbr>hypotonic fluids.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 4\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">D — Disability\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Check:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>GCS,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pupils,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>limb power,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>speech,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>seizure activity,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>random blood glucose,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>swallowing risk.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypoglycemia must be excluded because it can mimic stroke.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">E — Exposure\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Look for trauma, fever, infection, anticoagulant use, pressure injury risk, DVT risk, dehydration,\u003cbr>and signs of bleeding elsewhere.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">6. CT Brain: The Key Investigation\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The most important investigation is:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Urgent non-contrast CT brain\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Do not give aspirin, clopidogrel, heparin, warfarin, DOACs, or thrombolysis before hemorrhage\u003cbr>is excluded. Non-contrast CT rapidly differentiates hemorrhagic from ischemic stroke.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CT findings in acute intracerebral hemorrhage\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Acute blood appears hyperdense/bright on non-contrast CT.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The CT report should document:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. hemorrhage location,\u003cbr>2. approximate hematoma volume,\u003cbr>3. intraventricular extension,\u003cbr>4. surrounding edema,\u003cbr>5. mass effect,\u003cbr>6. midline shift,\u003cbr>7. hydrocephalus,\u003cbr>8. brainstem compression,\u003cbr>9. Herniation signs,\u003cbr>10. posterior fossa involvement.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Typical hypertensive CT pattern\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 5\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypertensive ICH commonly occurs in:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. putamen/basal ganglia,   2. thalamus,   3. pons,   4. cerebellum.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Lobar hemorrhage pattern\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Lobar hemorrhage suggests:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>1. cerebral amyloid angiopathy\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>2. tumor,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>3. AVM,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>4. anticoagulant-related hemorrhage,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>5. hemorrhagic transformation.\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">When to do CT angiography\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Request CT angiography when there is suspicion of:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. aneurysm,\u003cbr>2. AVM,\u003cbr>3. young patient with ICH,\u003cbr>4. lobar bleeds without hypertension,\u003cbr>5. subarachnoid hemorrhage,\u003cbr>6. unusual hemorrhage location,\u003cbr>7. disproportionate edema/mass lesion.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The AHA/ASA work-up emphasizes CT/CTA where indicated, especially when etiology is\u003cbr>uncertain or vascular lesion is suspected.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">7. Laboratory Findings Needed\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Do labs urgently, but do not delay CT or stabilization.\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>INVESTIGATION\u003c/td>\u003ctd>REASON\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>RBG\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Excludes hypoglycemia/stroke mimic\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>FBP/CBC\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Hb, infection, platelets\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Platelet count\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Low platelets worsen bleeding and affect surgery\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>PT/INR\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Warfarin effect, liver disease, coagulopathy\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>aPTT\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Heparin effect/coagulation disorder\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Urea/creatinine/electrolytes\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Renal function, sodium, potassium\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>LFTs\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Liver disease/coagulopathy\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Blood group and crossmatch\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Surgery/transfusion readiness\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 6\u003c/div>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>ECG\u003c/td>\u003ctd>AF, ischemia, arrhythmia\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Troponin\u003c/td>\u003ctd>If chest pain/ECG changes/stroke-heart syndrome\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Toxicology\u003c/td>\u003ctd>If stimulant/cocaine suspected\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Pregnancy test\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Women of reproductive age\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Findings that change management immediately include high INR, low platelets, renal failure,\u003cbr>severe sodium abnormality, hypoglycemia, severe hyperglycemia, and anticoagulant\u003cbr>exposure.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">GCS — essential\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">GCS is critical in hemorrhagic stroke. It determines airway risk, ICU need, deterioration, and  prognosis.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Urgent senior/ICU/neurosurgical review is needed if:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  GCS ≤8,   •  falling GCS,   •  unequal pupils,   •  abnormal breathing,   •  signs of herniation.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ICH Score — appropriate prognostic score\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ICH score is more appropriate than CHA₂DS₂-VASc for hemorrhagic stroke prognosis.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It uses:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  GCS,   •  age ≥80 years,   •  infratentorial origin,   •  hematoma volume ≥30 mL,   •  intraventricular extension.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Higher score suggests worse prognosis. However, the AHA/ASA guideline warns that severity\u003cbr>scores should not be used as the sole basis to limit life-sustaining treatment.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">AF patients when balancing future ischemic stroke risk against recurrent hemorrhage risk.”\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">STEPWISE MANAGEMENT\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 1: Stabilize first using ABCDE\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 7\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The patient should be stabilized before extensive discussion. Protect the airway, maintain\u003cbr>oxygenation, avoid hypotension, check glucose, control seizures if present, and prepare for\u003cbr>urgent CT.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If GCS is low, airway unsafe, or respiratory pattern abnormal, ICU/anesthesia should be  involved early.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 2: Urgent CT brain\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Do urgent non-contrast CT brain.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 3: Admit to ICU/HDU/stroke unit\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">All acute ICH patients should be admitted to a monitored setting where neurological status, BP,\u003cbr>airway, seizures, and complications can be observed. Tanzania STG-based guidance supports\u003cbr>ICU or stroke-unit admission for acute hemorrhagic stroke, and your uploaded notes also\u003cbr>emphasize monitored care for low GCS, IVH, hydrocephalus, seizures, raised ICP, and\u003cbr>anticoagulant-associated hemorrhage.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Admit urgently if there is:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">❖ low/falling GCS,\u003cbr>❖ large hematoma,\u003cbr>❖ IVH,\u003cbr>❖ hydrocephalus,\u003cbr>❖ cerebellar hemorrhage,\u003cbr>❖ uncontrolled BP,\u003cbr>❖ seizures,\u003cbr>❖ anticoagulant-related bleed,\u003cbr>❖ respiratory compromise,\u003cbr>❖ raised ICP signs.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. BLOOD PRESSURE MANAGEMENT\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">BP control is one of the most important acute treatments because high BP contributes to\u003cbr>hematoma expansion. However, BP should be lowered smoothly, not abruptly.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Target\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">For many patients with mild-to-moderate ICH and SBP 150–220 mmHg, it is reasonable to\u003cbr>lower SBP toward around 140 mmHg, provided treatment is smooth and avoids hypotension.\u003cbr>AHA/ASA emphasizes smooth sustained BP control and avoiding BP variability.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Avoid sudden normalization of BP. Do not drop BP excessively because cerebral perfusion may  worsen.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 8\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If IV labetalol is available\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Give:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. Labetalol 20 mg IV slowly over 2 minutes\u003cbr>2. Repeat 40 mg IV after 10 minutes if BP remains high\u003cbr>3. Then 80 mg IV every 10 minutes as needed\u003cbr>4. Maximum total dose: 300 mg\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Avoid or use caution in:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">severe asthma/COPD with bronchospasm,\u003cbr>Bradycardia,\u003cbr>heart block,\u003cbr>acute decompensated heart failure/pulmonary edema.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If labetalol/nicardipine is unavailable\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Use:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. Hydralazine 5–10 mg IV slowly\u003cbr>2. Repeat every 20–30 minutes\u003cbr>3. Monitor closely for excessive BP drop and reflex tachycardia.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hydralazine is commonly used in Tanzania because it is available, but it is less predictable than\u003cbr>labetalol or nicardipine.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Avoid\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">short-acting sublingual nifedipine,\u003cbr>sudden BP normalization,\u003cbr>hypotension,\u003cbr>unnecessary aggressive diuresis unless pulmonary edema is present.\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>4.\u003c/td>\u003ctd>STOP ANTITHROMBOTICS IMMEDIATELY\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Stop all drugs that can worsen bleeding:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>1. aspirin,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>2. clopidogrel,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>3. warfarin,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>4. heparin,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>5. enoxaparin,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>6. rivaroxaban\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>7. apixaban,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 9\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Do not start acute antiplatelet therapy in confirmed ICH.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">5.  Reverse Anticoagulation If Present\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Anticoagulant-associated ICH is an emergency. Reversal should be started urgently once drug  exposure is identified.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Warfarin-associated ICH\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If INR is elevated:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">AHA/ASA preferred where available\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  4-factor PCC + IV vitamin K\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">PCC is preferred because it reverses faster and with less volume than FFP.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If PCC is unavailable:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. withhold warfarin,\u003cbr>2. give vitamin K 10 mg IV slowly,\u003cbr>3. consider FFP while arranging senior/neurosurgical input.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Heparin-associated ICH\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Stop heparin.   •  Give protamine sulfate according to recent heparin exposure.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dabigatran-associated ICH\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Give idarucizumab 5 g IV if available.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>If unavailable and severe renal failure/drug accumulation exists, supportive care and\u003cbr>dialysis may be discussed.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Apixaban/rivaroxaban-associated ICH\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Give Andexanet alfa if available.   •  If unavailable, consider 4-factor PCC according to local protocol.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In many Tanzania settings, specific DOAC reversal agents may not be available, so practical\u003cbr>management may rely on stopping the drug, supportive care, PCC if available, and specialist\u003cbr>input.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">6.  RAISED INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE MANAGEMENT\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Suspect raised ICP if there is:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 10\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. falling GCS,\u003cbr>2. worsening headache/vomiting,\u003cbr>3. unequal pupils,\u003cbr>4. Cushing response,\u003cbr>5. papilledema,\u003cbr>6. CT mass effect,\u003cbr>7. midline shift,\u003cbr>8. hydrocephalus,\u003cbr>9. herniation signs.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">General measures\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. Elevate head of bed to 30 degrees.\u003cbr>2. Keep neck midline.\u003cbr>3. Avoid tight collars or tight ETT ties.\u003cbr>4. Avoid hypoxia.\u003cbr>5. Avoid hypercapnia.\u003cbr>6. Treat fever.\u003cbr>7. Treat seizures.\u003cbr>8. Avoid hypotonic fluids.\u003cbr>9. Use isotonic saline if fluids are needed.\u003cbr>10. hemorrhagic stroke drafts, but i have corrected the parts that should not be overused clinically. the key correction is this: cha₂ds₂-vasc is not used for acute hemorrhagic stroke management, and nihss is not the main hemorrhagic stroke decision- making score. in acute intracerebral hemorrhage, the most important clinical decision tools are gcs, ct findings, hematoma volume/location, intraventricular extension, hydrocephalus, mass effect, anticoagulant use, and ich score. hemorrhagic stroke is an acute neurological deficit caused by bleeding within the cranial cavity. it is mainly divided into intracerebral hemorrhage, where bleeding occurs into the brain parenchyma, and subarachnoid hemorrhage, where bleeding occurs into the subarachnoid space, commonly due to aneurysmal rupture. this master note focuses on spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage, because this is the common hypertensive hemorrhagic stroke usually managed in internal medicine, emergencies, icu, and neurosurgical settings. the 2022 aha/asa guideline defines spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage as non-traumatic bleeding into the brain parenchyma and emphasizes rapid diagnosis, bp control, reversal of coagulopathy, neurosurgical assessment, icp management, and stroke-unit/icu care. hemorrhagic stroke kills through two mechanisms. first, the hematoma directly destroys brain tissue. second, the expanding hematoma causes raised intracranial pressure, perihematomal edema, hydrocephalus, midline shift, herniation, and brainstem compression. the aha/asa clinical update describes early injury from hematoma expansion and later secondary injury from edema, inflammation, and blood product toxicity. common causes of hemorrhagic stroke the commonest cause in many african/tanzania ward settings is poorly controlled chronic hypertension, especially with poor adherence to antihypertensive medication. hypertensive hemorrhage classically occurs in deep brain structures supplied by small penetrating arteries. important causes include: cause typical clue chronic hypertension deep hemorrhage: basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum cerebral amyloid angiopathy elderly patient, lobar hemorrhage warfarin/doac/heparin anticoagulant history, high inr if warfarin antiplatelet therapy aspirin/clopidogrel may worsen bleeding avm/aneurysm/cavernoma young patient, lobar/unusual site, sah component brain tumor bleed lobar hemorrhage with edema/mass lesion coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia liver disease, dic, hematologic disease cocaine/amphetamine severe acute hypertension, young patient hemorrhagic transformation recent ischemic stroke/thrombolysis/large infarct in kcmc/tanzania practical assessment, first ask about hypertension, adherence, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, alcohol, ckd, trauma, previous stroke, and age. in a young patient, lobar bleed, or unusual location, think harder about avm, aneurysm, venous thrombosis, tumor, or vasculitis. 4. clinical presentation hemorrhagic stroke may present with sudden focal neurological deficit, severe headache, vomiting, seizures, reduced consciousness, severe hypertension, or signs of raised intracranial pressure. compared with ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke more commonly presents with headache, vomiting, early reduced gcs, seizures, and very high bp, although clinical features alone cannot reliably differentiate the two. site-based clinical clues hemorrhage site clinical pattern basal ganglia/internal contralateral hemiparesis, facial weakness, sensory loss, gaze capsule deviation thalamus sensory loss, reduced consciousness, vertical gaze palsy cerebellum vomiting, vertigo, ataxia, headache, rapid deterioration if hydrocephalus pons coma, pinpoint pupils, quadriparesis, abnormal respiration lobar cortex seizures, aphasia, neglect, visual field defect depending on lobe intraventricular extension reduced gcs, hydrocephalus, raised icp cerebellar and pontine hemorrhages are especially dangerous because small volumes can rapidly compress the brainstem. 5. immediate diagnostic evaluation step 1: start with abcde do not begin by writing a long clerking note. start by deciding whether the patient is dying. a — airway assess whether the patient can protect the airway. call icu/anesthesia early if there is: • gcs ≤8, • recurrent vomiting, • aspiration risk, • bulbar dysfunction, • uncontrolled seizures, • brainstem signs, • worsening consciousness. if airway is unsafe, intubation may be required before ct. b — breathing check respiratory rate, spo₂, breathing pattern, aspiration, and chest findings. give oxygen if hypoxic. avoid hypoxia and hypercapnia because both increase secondary brain injury and may worsen icp. usual target spo₂ is >94%, but if copd/co₂ retention risk is present, use 88–92%. c — circulation insert two iv lines. monitor bp, pulse, ecg, capillary refill, temperature, and urine output. avoid hypotension because it worsens cerebral perfusion. use isotonic fluids if needed. avoid hypotonic fluids. d — disability check: • gcs, • pupils, • limb power, • speech, • seizure activity, • random blood glucose, • swallowing risk. hypoglycemia must be excluded because it can mimic stroke. e — exposure look for trauma, fever, infection, anticoagulant use, pressure injury risk, dvt risk, dehydration, and signs of bleeding elsewhere. 6. ct brain: the key investigation the most important investigation is: urgent non-contrast ct brain do not give aspirin, clopidogrel, heparin, warfarin, doacs, or thrombolysis before hemorrhage is excluded. non-contrast ct rapidly differentiates hemorrhagic from ischemic stroke. ct findings in acute intracerebral hemorrhage acute blood appears hyperdense/bright on non-contrast ct. the ct report should document: 1. hemorrhage location, 2. approximate hematoma volume, 3. intraventricular extension, 4. surrounding edema, 5. mass effect, 6. midline shift, 7. hydrocephalus, 8. brainstem compression, 9. herniation signs, 10. posterior fossa involvement. typical hypertensive ct pattern hypertensive ich commonly occurs in: 1. putamen/basal ganglia, 2. thalamus, 3. pons, 4. cerebellum. lobar hemorrhage pattern lobar hemorrhage suggests: 1. cerebral amyloid angiopathy, 2. tumor, 3. avm, 4. anticoagulant-related hemorrhage, 5. hemorrhagic transformation. when to do ct angiography request ct angiography when there is suspicion of: 1. aneurysm, 2. avm, 3. young patient with ich, 4. lobar bleeds without hypertension, 5. subarachnoid hemorrhage, 6. unusual hemorrhage location, 7. disproportionate edema/mass lesion. the aha/asa work-up emphasizes ct/cta where indicated, especially when etiology is uncertain or vascular lesion is suspected. 7. laboratory findings needed do labs urgently, but do not delay ct or stabilization. investigation reason rbg excludes hypoglycemia/stroke mimic fbp/cbc hb, infection, platelets platelet count low platelets worsen bleeding and affect surgery pt/inr warfarin effect, liver disease, coagulopathy aptt heparin effect/coagulation disorder urea/creatinine/electrolytes renal function, sodium, potassium lfts liver disease/coagulopathy blood group and crossmatch surgery/transfusion readiness ecg af, ischemia, arrhythmia troponin if chest pain/ecg changes/stroke-heart syndrome toxicology if stimulant/cocaine suspected pregnancy test women of reproductive age findings that change management immediately include high inr, low platelets, renal failure, severe sodium abnormality, hypoglycemia, severe hyperglycemia, and anticoagulant exposure. gcs — essential gcs is critical in hemorrhagic stroke. it determines airway risk, icu need, deterioration, and prognosis. urgent senior/icu/neurosurgical review is needed if: • gcs ≤8, • falling gcs, • unequal pupils, • abnormal breathing, • signs of herniation. ich score — appropriate prognostic score ich score is more appropriate than cha₂ds₂-vasc for hemorrhagic stroke prognosis. it uses: • gcs, • age ≥80 years, • infratentorial origin, • hematoma volume ≥30 ml, • intraventricular extension. higher score suggests worse prognosis. however, the aha/asa guideline warns that severity scores should not be used as the sole basis to limit life-sustaining treatment. af patients when balancing future ischemic stroke risk against recurrent hemorrhage risk.” stepwise management step 1: stabilize first using abcde the patient should be stabilized before extensive discussion. protect the airway, maintain oxygenation, avoid hypotension, check glucose, control seizures if present, and prepare for urgent ct. if gcs is low, airway unsafe, or respiratory pattern abnormal, icu/anesthesia should be involved early. step 2: urgent ct brain do urgent non-contrast ct brain. step 3: admit to icu/hdu/stroke unit all acute ich patients should be admitted to a monitored setting where neurological status, bp, airway, seizures, and complications can be observed. tanzania stg-based guidance supports icu or stroke-unit admission for acute hemorrhagic stroke, and your uploaded notes also emphasize monitored care for low gcs, ivh, hydrocephalus, seizures, raised icp, and anticoagulant-associated hemorrhage. admit urgently if there is: ❖ low/falling gcs, ❖ large hematoma, ❖ ivh, ❖ hydrocephalus, ❖ cerebellar hemorrhage, ❖ uncontrolled bp, ❖ seizures, ❖ anticoagulant-related bleed, ❖ respiratory compromise, ❖ raised icp signs. 4. blood pressure management bp control is one of the most important acute treatments because high bp contributes to hematoma expansion. however, bp should be lowered smoothly, not abruptly. target for many patients with mild-to-moderate ich and sbp 150–220 mmhg, it is reasonable to lower sbp toward around 140 mmhg, provided treatment is smooth and avoids hypotension. aha/asa emphasizes smooth sustained bp control and avoiding bp variability. avoid sudden normalization of bp. do not drop bp excessively because cerebral perfusion may worsen. if iv labetalol is available give: 1. labetalol 20 mg iv slowly over 2 minutes 2. repeat 40 mg iv after 10 minutes if bp remains high 3. then 80 mg iv every 10 minutes as needed 4. maximum total dose: 300 mg avoid or use caution in: severe asthma/copd with bronchospasm, bradycardia, heart block, acute decompensated heart failure/pulmonary edema. if labetalol/nicardipine is unavailable use: 1. hydralazine 5–10 mg iv slowly 2. repeat every 20–30 minutes 3. monitor closely for excessive bp drop and reflex tachycardia. hydralazine is commonly used in tanzania because it is available, but it is less predictable than labetalol or nicardipine. avoid short-acting sublingual nifedipine, sudden bp normalization, hypotension, unnecessary aggressive diuresis unless pulmonary edema is present. 4. stop antithrombotics immediately stop all drugs that can worsen bleeding: 1. aspirin, 2. clopidogrel, 3. warfarin, 4. heparin, 5. enoxaparin, 6. rivaroxaban, 7. apixaban, 8. dabigatran. do not start acute antiplatelet therapy in confirmed ich. 5. reverse anticoagulation if present anticoagulant-associated ich is an emergency. reversal should be started urgently once drug exposure is identified. warfarin-associated ich if inr is elevated: aha/asa preferred where available • 4-factor pcc + iv vitamin k pcc is preferred because it reverses faster and with less volume than ffp. if pcc is unavailable: 1. withhold warfarin, 2. give vitamin k 10 mg iv slowly, 3. consider ffp while arranging senior/neurosurgical input. heparin-associated ich • stop heparin. • give protamine sulfate according to recent heparin exposure. dabigatran-associated ich • give idarucizumab 5 g iv if available. • if unavailable and severe renal failure/drug accumulation exists, supportive care and dialysis may be discussed. apixaban/rivaroxaban-associated ich • give andexanet alfa if available. • if unavailable, consider 4-factor pcc according to local protocol. in many tanzania settings, specific doac reversal agents may not be available, so practical management may rely on stopping the drug, supportive care, pcc if available, and specialist input. 6. raised intracranial pressure management suspect raised icp if there is: 1. falling gcs, 2. worsening headache/vomiting, 3. unequal pupils, 4. cushing response, 5. papilledema, 6. ct mass effect, 7. midline shift, 8. hydrocephalus, 9. herniation signs. general measures 1. elevate head of bed to 30 degrees. 2. keep neck midline. 3. avoid tight collars or tight ett ties. 4. avoid hypoxia. 5. avoid hypercapnia. 6. treat fever. 7. treat seizures. 8. avoid hypotonic fluids. 9. use isotonic saline if fluids are needed. 10. call neurosurgery urgently if hydrocephalus, mass effect, posterior fossa bleed, or deterioration is present. osmotherapy use osmotherapy only when there is clinical/radiological evidence of raised icp, not routinely for every ich. options: 1. mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg iv bolus, repeated depending on response and renal function. 2. 3% hypertonic saline, where available, according to local protocol. monitor: 1. serum sodium, 2. serum osmolality, 3. renal function, 4. urine output, 5. neurological response. avoid mannitol in severe hypotension, severe dehydration, or significant renal failure unless specialist guided. 6. evd: external ventricular drainage is a neurosurgical catheter inserted into the ventricular system to drain csf, reduce obstructive hydrocephalus, monitor icp, and relieve pressure. evd is not for every hemorrhagic stroke evd is indicated mainly when there is: • intraventricular hemorrhage with obstructive hydrocephalus, • reduced consciousness due to hydrocephalus, • raised icp needing csf immediate surgical removal of cerebellar hemorrhage, with or without evd, when these high- risk features are present. supratentorial hemorrhage routine craniotomy for supratentorial ich has uncertain antiseizure drugs in ich patients without seizures because there is no proven benefit. practical regimen if actively convulsing: • diazepam 10 mg iv slowly, or • lorazepam 4 mg iv if available. then fluids, and general icu care fever; treat fever aggressively because it worsens brain injury. use paracetamol, cooling measures, and search for infection. glucose; avoid both hypoglycemia and severe hyperglycemia. hypoglycemia mimics stroke; hyperglycemia is associated with worse outcomes. avoid overly tight glucose control that causes hypoglycemia. fluids; use isotonic fluids. avoid hypotonic fluids because they worsen cerebral edema. avoid dehydration and hypotension but also avoid unnecessary fluid overload. 18. swallowing and nutrition do not feed orally until swallowing is assessed. if reasonable to prevent recurrence. depending on comorbidity and renal function: a. amlodipine 5–10 mg po once daily b. losartan 50–100 mg po once daily, or enalapril 5 mg po once/twice daily c. hydrochlorothiazide 12.5–25 mg po once daily d. spironolactone 25 mg po once daily for resistant hypertension if egfr and potassium allow. avoid recurrence factors 1. poor bp adherence, 2. nsaid overuse, 3. heavy alcohol, 4. smoking, 5. uncontrolled diabetes, 6. ckd progression, 7. anticoagulant overdose, 8. recurrent falls."},{"id":"pdf-6","disease":"Hypertension","label":"Diagnosis and src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 1\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">HYPERTENSION\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Definition\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypertension is a chronic elevation of systemic arterial blood pressure. In most adult clinical\u003cbr>settings, hypertension is diagnosed when repeated blood pressure readings are ≥140/90 mmHg,\u003cbr>while the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline defines high blood pressure from ≥130/80 mmHg and\u003cbr>recommends treatment targets generally below 130/80 mmHg for most adults.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In Tanzania/KCMC practice, diagnosis and treatment often follow the practical public-health\u003cbr>threshold of BP ≥140/90 mmHg, consistent with WHO and Tanzania STG approaches. WHO\u003cbr>recommends starting pharmacological treatment for confirmed hypertension at SBP ≥140 mmHg\u003cbr>or DBP ≥90 mmHg, and earlier treatment at SBP 130–139 mmHg if the patient has\u003cbr>cardiovascular disease, diabetes, CKD, or high cardiovascular risk.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Classification\u003c/h4>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Category\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>BP level\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Normal\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>&lt;120/&lt;80 mmHg\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Elevated / high-normal\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>120–129/&lt;80 mmHg\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Stage 1 hypertension\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>130–139 or 80–89 mmHg\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Stage 2 hypertension\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>≥140 or ≥90 mmHg\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Severe hypertension\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>≥180 and/or ≥120 mmHg\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 2\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In ward work, always separate uncomplicated hypertension from hypertensive emergency.\u003cbr>Hypertensive emergency means severe BP elevation with acute target-organ damage, such as\u003cbr>stroke, pulmonary edema, ACS, AKI, aortic dissection, encephalopathy, or eclampsia.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Risk Factors\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Common risk factors include age, obesity, high salt intake, alcohol use, smoking, physical\u003cbr>inactivity, diabetes, CKD, dyslipidemia, family history, obstructive sleep apnea, and chronic\u003cbr>NSAID/steroid use.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In Tanzania, also think of poor treatment adherence, late diagnosis, limited home BP monitoring,\u003cbr>high dietary salt, alcohol, obesity, CKD, and secondary causes in young patients.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Clinical Features\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Most patients are asymptomatic. Symptoms, when present, may include headache, dizziness,\u003cbr>palpitations, visual symptoms, chest pain, dyspnea, or features of complications.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Look specifically for target-organ damage: LVH/heart failure, stroke/TIA, CKD/proteinuria,\u003cbr>hypertensive retinopathy, peripheral vascular disease, and coronary artery disease.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Diagnostic Evaluation\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Confirm BP properly using correct cuff size, patient seated and rested, arm supported, and\u003cbr>repeated measurements. Diagnosis should not be made from one reading unless there is\u003cbr>hypertensive emergency.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Proper BP Measurement — Diagnostic Evaluation\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Accurate BP measurement is part of diagnosis. A wrong position, wrong cuff, talking, full\u003cbr>bladder, or measuring immediately after walking can falsely raise BP and may lead to\u003cbr>overdiagnosis or unnecessary treatment. AHA guidance emphasizes seated, rested, quiet\u003cbr>measurement with the arm supported at heart level, feet flat, and cuff on bare skin.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Before measuring BP\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The patient should avoid the following for at least 30 minutes before measurement:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Avoid before BP\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Why\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Caffeine/coffee/energy drinks\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Can transiently raise BP\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Smoking/nicotine\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Sympathetic stimulation raises BP\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Exercise/walking fast\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Raises BP temporarily\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Full bladder\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Can falsely elevate BP\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Talking/phone use\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Can falsely elevate reading\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 3\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Before taking BP, ask the patient to sit quietly and rest for at least 5 minutes. AHA home BP\u003cbr>instructions specifically advise no caffeine, smoking, or exercise within 30 minutes, emptying\u003cbr>the bladder, and resting quietly for 5 minutes before measurement.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. CDC gives the\u003cbr>same core steps: no\u003cbr>talking, cuff on bare\u003cbr>skin, back supported,\u003cbr>feet flat, and arm at\u003cbr>chest/heart height.\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 4\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,
